migration_summary: Drop the nickname column from the City model, one migration after it was added (0018_city_nickname) and populated. Converted faithfully from the real Django RemoveField operation to the single equivalent PostgreSQL DDL statement it generates.
migration_sql: ALTER TABLE api_city DROP COLUMN nickname;
schema_summary: api_city is a small reference/lookup table (cities available in the app), not a high-write operational table.

risk_flags.message: DROP COLUMN is destructive and irreversible without a backup or a preserved down-migration; any application code, serializer, or admin view still reading api_city.nickname breaks immediately on deploy.

risk_narrative: This project's own migration history shows the field being added (0018) and then removed four migrations later (0022) — a real example of a column that was added, never fully adopted, and cleaned up. Even on a small table, the operation itself is unconditionally destructive: the data is gone the moment the migration runs, and Django's own reverse migration for RemoveField is a no-op (there is no way to regenerate the dropped values), so 'rollback' here really means 're-add an empty column', not 'restore the data'.
lessons_learned: DROP COLUMN risk is about irreversibility of the data, not about table size or lock duration — a tiny table doesn't make a destructive change safe, it just makes the blast radius small. Confirm nothing (application code, reports, exports) still reads a column before dropping it, since the migration tool cannot warn about consumers outside its own schema history.

prediction_summary.risk_explanation: Fast on a small table, but the data itself is unrecoverable once the column is dropped.

dimension_details.note: Real production migration from Travel Mate server's Django migration set (api/migrations); migration_sql is the exact PostgreSQL DDL Django's migration executor generates for this RemoveField operation.
